ranking.note: Raised to P1: release-binary verification accepting revoked/expired keys is a responsibly disclosed security flaw in tooling operators rely on, the clearest category-critical item here.
Raised to P2 and moved up for consistency with #36105: both are the same class of supported-platform failure of the bitcoin wrapper, and this one makes the wrapper fail outright on common distros.
Moved up: silently dropping script flags and emitting a bare script with exit 0 is a correctness defect in a transaction-building tool, which this category ranks just after deployment tooling.

Raised from P4: the card describes options after positional arguments being silently swallowed across bitcoin-cli/-wallet/-tx (including -rpcwallet routing), a real user-facing footgun, not merely an incidental bitcoin-tx follow-up.
Moved up: a reproducible infinite hang is a concrete user-visible bug and outranks developer-convenience work in this band.
Moved down: a new developer/researcher convenience subcommand ranks below the tool bugs and silent-misparse fixes above it.
Moved down: measurable but internal developer speedup of a fuzz-coverage helper, below user-facing tool correctness.
Moved down: internal developer dependency-check script; maintenance payoff is real but narrow compared with the tool fixes above.
Lowered to P4: speculative internal clang-tidy refactor aid whose author states a preference for abandoning it in favour of a different approach.

inconsistencies: Chain: #36190 only tests behaviour introduced by #36105; review #36105 first, as the test PR has no value until the runtime fix lands.
Chain: #19460 depends on #10102 and #29409 and in turn unblocks #19461; its value is contingent on the earlier multiprocess PRs being accepted, so it should not be reviewed ahead of them.

#35831 (ArgsManager GNU-style parsing, which also changes how bitcoin-tx consumes arguments) and #36368 (bitcoin-tx rejecting over-separated in/outscript arguments) both touch bitcoin-tx argument handling and may conflict; #35831 is the broader change and settles the parsing model, so it should be reviewed first.

#35994 is effectively self-superseded: the author prefers manual declarative rewrites over the clang-tidy check in this PR, and the mechanical application introduced a witness-dropping bug, so a decision to close or redirect is what is needed rather than line review.
#36105 and #36106 are two independent breakages of the same tool (the bitcoin wrapper) on different platforms; they should be banded and handled together rather than one P2 and one P3.
result.notes: Band spread is deliberate: one security-grade item (#36293), two supported-platform failures of the bitcoin wrapper (P2), a broad P3 middle of tool bugs and developer utilities, and one effectively abandoned refactor at P4. Within P3 the ordering follows the category's own priority: deployment/transaction-touching correctness first, then widely used developer productivity tooling, then niche contrib prototypes.
